bib.title: Experimentation in action: Testing and evaluating a project (chapter 6, Machine Learning Engineering in Action)
bib.venue: Manning (book chapter; author/year not printed in chapter PDF, taken from caller)

question: How should an ML team rapidly test candidate approaches, score them uniformly, and pick one for an MVP without under- or over-investing in prototyping?
hypothesis: A time-boxed middle-ground prototyping phase with standardised metrics and visuals, and selection on more than accuracy, lowers the chance of project failure or cancellation.
contributions: Shared utilities: baseline smoothing plots, standard metric function, prediction plot, chronological split with check
Worked rapid tests of VAR, ARIMA and Holt-Winters on JFK passengers

limits: No benchmark or controlled experiment: one fictional scenario with illustrative plots; MAPE values are single holdout splits (split date 2006-07-08), no seeds or intervals.
Only three of nine tested models shown; others (VAR, elastic net, lasso, RNN) dropped as overwhelmingly poor, with no numbers.
Experience-based guidance (100 discarded attempts, success rates) is anecdotal.
Code uses statsmodels 0.11.1/0.12 APIs and pandas 'seaborn' style; dated. The ARIMA listing plots test['Domestic Passengers'] for the international series (likely typo in book).
Experiment tracking is deferred to chapter 7 (MLflow); this chapter only says to log, not how.
practices: Time-box prototyping to hours or a day per approach; test multiple approaches rather than one or all (Fig 6.1, sec 6.1.2).
Standardise metrics, splits, plots and baselines in shared code before teams diverge (6.1.1).
Always compute and record all agreed metrics (MAE, MAPE, MSE, RMSE, explained variance, R2) so past runs can be re-judged; do not argue over a single metric (6.1.1).
Compare against simple baselines (moving average, exponential smoothing) on the holdout (6.1.1).
Use deterministic chronological splits with an assertion that no rows are dropped or duplicated (listing 6.8).
Do not print metrics in functions; return dicts and log or persist them (MLflow in next chapter) (6.1.1 sidebar).
Do not abandon an approach after default-config failure, nor tune it for weeks; read API docs and match the installed library version (6.1.2).
Use a neutral moderator across prototyping teams to share findings (6.1.2 sidebar).
Keep experiment notebooks clean: delete dead code, no out-of-order cells (6.1.2 sidebar).

Score candidates in a decision matrix (accuracy, tuning sensitivity, implementation difficulty, training cost, inference cost, team familiarity), blind vote on teams' non-own solutions, DS lead veto on resourcing/complexity/cost (Fig 6.11, 6.12).
Show the business only viable candidates; summarise failures as 'we tried 15 other things' (6.2.1).
Before building ask: refresh frequency/SLA, data location, forecast storage, code base, training and inference location, delivery to users, reusable code, cadence (6.2.2).

def mape(y_true, y_pred):
    return np.mean(np.abs((y_true - y_pred) / y_true)) * 100

def split_correctness(data, train, test):
    assert data.size == train.size + test.size, \
    "Train count {} and test count {} did not match to source count {}".format(train.size, test.size, data.size)
def generate_splits(data, date):
    parsed_date = parse(date, fuzzy=True)
    nearest_date = data[:parsed_date].iloc(0)[-1].name
    train = data[:nearest_date]
    test = data[nearest_date:][1:]
    split_correctness(data, train, test)
    return train, test

def calculate_errors(y_true, y_pred):
    error_scores = {}
    mse = mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)
    error_scores['mae'] = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
    error_scores['mape'] = mape(y_true, y_pred)
    error_scores['mse'] = mse
    error_scores['rmse'] = sqrt(mse)
    error_scores['explained_var'] = explained_variance_score(y_true, y_pred)
    error_scores['r2'] = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)
    return error_scores
